item.title: Do People Trust AI Assistants Even When They Are Consistently Wrong?
item.description: arXiv:2611.14833v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: People are increasingly using conversational AI systems to make decisions despite concerns around their reliability. How well do people calibrate to AI systems' accuracy in multi-turn conversations? We measure how people's reliance on LLMs' advice changes across repeated interactions, varying whether the AI assistant is helpful (100% accurate), unhelpful (0% accurate), or mixed (50% accurate). Across 4 experiments, we find people learn to trust helpful models more than unhelpful ones (67% vs 21% of the time), but only when they receive external feedback on the models' accuracy. Without feedback, people continue to be persuaded 48% of the time by a consistently unhelpful model (vs 38% for helpful). Rather than gaining trust in helpful models, participant reliance on LLM advisors tended to be high in early trials and only fell with evidence of inaccuracy. Participants trusted LLM advisors more than they trusted human advisors (83% vs 65%, Experiment 4), and LLMs benefited more from having a helpful track record than humans did. In contrast with previous work, we find limited evidence of an advantage for arguing for the truth (versus a falsehood). Truth advantages emerged only when participants were already very confident in their position, and did not emerge at all for static hints. Collectively, the results suggest that people may be swayed by LLM advice, even when it is consistently false, unless they have access to timely ground-truth feedback. Unfortunately, in many domains such feedback may not be available, leading to overreliance on AI.
item.dc:creator: Cameron R. Jones, Julia Wong, Aaron S. Cohen, James Woolley, Benjamin K. Bergen

item.title: Branching Visual Inquiry in a Generative Visual Browser: A Matched Walkthrough Study
item.description: arXiv:2611.14862v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative visual browsers combine AI-generated visual pages with reader-selected branches rather than a fixed sequence. We analyzed eight author self-walkthroughs of Flipbook, organized as four pairs with identical starting prompts about sleep, vaccines, flight, and Pluto. Three paired routes differed at the first selection; the sleep routes separated after a shared repair-oriented opening. A route could remain locally coherent while narrowing to one mechanism or leaving part of its starting question unanswered. Some diagrams lacked sources. The analysis motivates three design directions: persistent path histories, prompts that reconnect a route to its starting question, and source or uncertainty cues for generated claims. It characterizes how one generative visual browser structured eight documented routes.
item.dc:creator: Hanjing Shi, Kimberly Wang, Dominic DiFranzo

item.title: Women's Genetic Health as Family Cooperative Work: Empirical Findings and a Case for Participatory AI
item.description: arXiv:2611.14871v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Genetics plays a significant role in women's health, with family members often experiencing shared symptoms or hereditary risks across generations. Yet health technologies, including emerging health AI tools, have supported women's health as an individual health practice. Drawing on a survey of 249 U.S. adult women, we characterize women's genetic health information work as cooperative work distributed across intergenerational family networks, identify who does this work and why, and document the barriers that fragment it. We find that generative AI use is a strong predictor of genetic health perception, but current tools focus on individuals rather than supporting collective coordination. We argue that designing AI for this domain requires participatory approaches that engage diverse women, healthcare professionals, and legal and community stakeholders, and we bring open design questions to the workshop.
item.dc:creator: Ziqi Yang, Yunan Chen, Daniel A. Epstein

item.title: Hear What You Eat: In-Ear Passive Acoustic Sensing for Multi-task Dietary Monitoring
item.description: arXiv:2611.14878v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The increasing obesity health concerns are driving the advancement of continuous dietary monitoring. Yet, existing single-sensor solutions still face challenges of coarse-grained sensing resolution, while multi-sensor fusion strategies encounter significant engineering complexity or hardware requirements. In our work, we present a single modality-based multi-dimensional dietary monitoring and logging solution, named EARDIET, which leverages inward-facing microphones on earables to capture in-ear chewing sounds for fine-grained diet analysis. With the texture audio profiles derivation, the pipeline consisting of signal processing and lightweight deep learning, is carefully designed to achieve eating episode detection, food texture sensing, and food type recognition simultaneously. Comprehensive experiments involving 32 participants with diverse BMI profiles are conducted to validate the effectiveness of multi-dimensional dietary monitoring. Compared with the state-of-the-art solutions, EARDIET can derive multi-dimensional dietary information with only a single modality, outperforming by about 10% in terms of eating episode detection. Furthermore, through real-world clinical validation, our solution can achieve masticatory disorder identification with an averaged F1-score of 85.97%, demonstrating potential for healthcare in the future.
item.dc:creator: Feiyu Han, Mingtian Zhu, Dawei Yan, Weiwei Jiang, Yuanhao Feng, Yanfei Zhang, Panlong Yang

item.title: Understanding the Effects of Multi-Agent Deliberation for Human-AI Decision-Making
item.description: arXiv:2611.14901v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent deliberation (MAD), where multiple LLMs engage in structured discussion, improves AI performance on many benchmarks, but whether it helps humans make better decisions remains untested. We conduct two user studies on LLM-response-verification and fact-checking. We first compare MAD against common AI decision-support methods that isolate its two defining dimensions --- multiple AIs and multi-round interaction. We find MAD outperformed single-round AI assistance on both tasks; multi-round interaction was the main driver of this benefit, while a second AI added value when the single AI had room to improve. Then, we study two design choices in MAD --- AI persona and human engagement level --- finding a devil's advocate persona to lower accuracy and user experience, while humans' active participation in MAD improved accuracy in one task at the cost of frustration. We conclude by discussing implications for when, why, and how multi-agent deliberation can support human decision-making.
item.dc:creator: Harry Yizhou Tian, Ming Yin

item.title: "It's still 100% on me": Designing AI Tools for the Intersection of Physicians' Care and Legal Infrastructures
item.description: arXiv:2611.14989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Laws and regulations deeply shape physicians' workflows and impact how they incorporate AI-based decision support tools to care for patients. Despite calls to comply with legal standards, many AI-based decision support tools have not transitioned well to clinical settings. The medical community remains concerned about their legal liability, risks to patients, and limited clinical value of such tools. To better understand how to address these concerns in the design of AI tools for clinical decision-making, we conducted 19 interviews with physicians in the U.S. We used scenario-based design to investigate physicians' legal concerns in the context of an AI-based drug recommendation tool. Drawing on the ethics of care, we surface connections between physicians' care and the healthcare laws and regulations that deeply shape their information needs. We describe how physicians wanted to use the tool in individual and collective practices to care for themselves, their patients, their colleagues, work institution, and even the broader medical profession. We discuss how the design of AI-based decision support tools can present legal ambiguities that would prevent their caring actions and lead to non-use of the AI tool. Through our work, we contribute to responsible AI development in healthcare. Our analysis illuminates why and how certain kinds of information reduce legal ambiguity and support physicians' care when using AI-based decision support tools. We contribute an understanding of how to help physicians navigate legal liability and draw implications for grounding AI tools' designs in their care.
item.dc:creator: Gennie Mansi, Julia Kim, Lynn Dombrowski, Mark Riedl, Naveena Karusala

item.title: Data Visualization Influencers: Tracing the Creation and Curation Strategies Behind Propagandist Visualizations on X
item.description: arXiv:2611.15042v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data visualization is increasingly understood as a political process shaped by creators' editorial design and data choices. Prior research has examined how such choices produce deceptive visualizations, focusing on social media users' misleading visualizations of public data. This overlooks how creators draw on professional expertise to produce propagandist visualizations of political narratives. We investigate visualization creators who design and share propagandist visualizations of political claims, such as immigration, criminality, and others, in US online discourse. Extending prior work on data visualization as propaganda, we present an exploratory study of 17 creators and the propagandist visualizations they create and curate for political discourse on X. We introduce the notion of a ``data visualization influencer'': an online creator who (1) leverages perceived credibility as a data expert, and (2) engages in epistemic capture of the credibility aesthetics of data and visualizations to manufacture propaganda. We discuss implications for research and practice.
item.dc:creator: Priya Dhawka, Nina Lutz

item.title: "I don't know what I don't know": Exploring the Benefits and Challenges of AI in Interdisciplinary Research
item.description: arXiv:2611.15121v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interdisciplinary research is widely lauded as beneficial for society but presents unique challenges to the researchers who bridge disciplinary boundaries. Despite the rapid increase in the availability and usage of AI systems for research tasks, there is little work studying how AI systems have impacted workflows that span unfamiliar disciplines. Through a survey ($N=62$) and follow-up interviews ($N=23$) with interdisciplinary researchers, we describe the unique challenges and opportunities for AI in interdisciplinary research workflows. Participants viewed AI both as a solution and exacerbation of the general challenge of "unknown unknowns": AI systems could facilitate a broad awareness of a new research area, yet also provide an illusion of understanding. Crucially, participants lacked the expertise and intuition to catch these illusions. Our findings motivate a focus on designing AI systems to support rather than automate collaboration across disciplines, scaffold learning opportunities, and include avenues for triangulation between resources.
item.dc:creator: Indu Panigrahi, Tal August

item.title: An Experience Report on Teaching Students to Evaluate AI Agent Skills as Authorization Decisions
item.description: arXiv:2611.15170v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cultivating a security mindset has long been a goal of computing education, and students now need it when deciding whether to trust an AI agent skill. Skills are add-ons that can shape an agent's behavior through natural language instructions and configuration settings, not just executable code. To prepare students to evaluate skills as authorization decisions, we designed a classroom activity and taught it in a senior undergraduate and a graduate cybersecurity-focused course. Students inspected three example skills, each pairing a real workflow task with one agent-specific authority, such as acting without asking for user consent before each action. The activity guided them to make initial authorization recommendations and then use a static security scanner to test and revise their recommendations. We observed in class that students needed guidance to extend their security review from a skill's code to what they would be authorizing the agent to do through the skill. Pre/post surveys from 11 volunteer respondents in this preliminary pilot showed greater self-reported confidence in evaluating skills, and post-activity responses placed more emphasis on the authority that skills carry. We release all activity materials for reuse.
item.dc:creator: Zikai Alex Wen, Donald Chinn, Yan Bai

item.title: Alignment De-Identifies Without Aligning: A Congruence-Invariant Relational Gap in Cross-Subject Neural Representations
item.description: arXiv:2611.15204v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In brain-computer interfaces, inter-subject variability remains a major challenge that limits decoding performance across users. Subject-wise alignment is widely used to improve cross-subject transfer of neural decoders, yet it is typically evaluated only through decoding accuracy, which cannot determine whether aligned representations share greater task-related structure. We therefore distinguish two questions that accuracy conflates: whether alignment removes subject-specific information and whether it makes the relational organization of task conditions more similar across individuals. Using three motor imagery-EEG cohorts, trials are represented as covariance matrices and aligned by recentering each subject's mean covariance to a common reference. Subject-specific information is quantified with a subject-identification probe, whereas relational structure is assessed using representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs) computed from condition means with the affine-invariant Riemannian distance. We show that recentering leaves this distance, and therefore the resulting RDMs, unchanged. Consistent with this result, recentering reduces subject identification accuracy from 0.96 to chance level across all cohorts, while altering RDMs only at numerical precision. Cross-subject agreement in relational structure is significantly above zero but below the estimator's lower noise ceiling. Introducing an explicit similarity regularizer during training also fails to increase held-out agreement: the apparent reduction in between-subject differences is explained by a decline in the reliability ceiling rather than improved alignment. These findings show that eliminating subject identity is not equivalent to aligning relational geometry. More broadly, alignment claims must be interpreted relative to the invariances of both the distance and the statistic used to evaluate them.
item.dc:creator: Anna Notaro (University of Tuebingen, Germany), Letizia Rossato (Technical University of Denmark, Denmark), Sadasivan Puthusserypady (Technical University of Denmark, Denmark)

item.title: Immersive Sight-Restriction-Based Collision Prevention Using Generic Particle Systems in Virtual Reality
item.description: arXiv:2611.15561v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Collision prevention systems (CPS) help VR users navigate their physical surroundings safely. Most approaches overlay conceptually distinct grids or add solid virtual counterparts of physical obstacles; both can reveal the physical space, as they either stand out visually or behave inconsistently during locomotion. We explore sight restriction as an alternative: a standard particle system visualizes the play area boundary as a fog-like cloud whose intensity scales with proximity and viewing direction. A pre-study (N=10) determined the distance at which the visualization must appear. In a main study (N=11), we compared this particle-based CPS with a grid-based solution, focusing on locomotion behavior: across 253 approach episodes, users interrupted their approach after a comparable distance once either visualization appeared. Although the particle boundary was visible three times as often, participants reported higher presence. We release our implementation as open source to support further work on immersive collision prevention.
item.dc:creator: Annalisa Degenhard, Annika Stampf, Michael Rietzler, Enrico Rukzio

item.title: Making Doula Coordination Breakdowns Visible: A Participatory Case Study
item.description: arXiv:2611.15580v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Doulas are trained, non-medical professionals who provide emotional, physical, and informational support to pregnant individuals before, during, and after childbirth. Doulas provide extensive relational and coordination labor for pregnant and postpartum patients, spending far more time with clients than traditional providers do, yet they operate with almost no doula-specific digital infrastructure. This gap is especially acute in rural communities, where postpartum depression affects about 25% of women, well above the national average, and where geographic isolation and provider shortages leave many without access to behavioral health care. DoulaConnect began as a 12-week evidence-based postpartum texting curriculum, piloted separately in a randomized controlled trial in rural New England. Building on that work, we present DoulaConnect's development into an AI-enabled platform co-designed with doulas and rural mothers through participatory human-centered design, as a case for surfacing where coordination breaks down in doula practice and who currently absorbs the resulting burden. Our community-based participatory study, conducted across the platform's Discover and Define phases, combines qualitative sessions with doulas and mothers to identify these breakdowns. We close with tensions this approach surfaces and open questions for the workshop about how these findings will inform future participatory AI infrastructure for doula care in rural and other under-resourced communities.
item.dc:creator: Emma Ricci-De Lucca, Saanvi Chilakapati, Jillian Berch, Ashley Kim, Sahithi Medikondla, Iha Rastogi, Margaret R. Emerson, Elizabeth L. Murnane, Karen L. Fortuna

item.title: Integrating Slides, Mathematics, and Simulation in One Page: GenAI-Assisted HTML Learning Objects for Engineering Courses
item.description: arXiv:2611.15686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Engineering courses spread their materials across slides (PPTX), typeset notes (LaTeX/PDF), and MATLAB, leaving students to connect them. We describe an instructor-in-the-loop workflow in which generative AI (GenAI) converts these assets into single-file HTML learning objects that combine presentation, mathematics, visualization, simulation, and assessment; a page is released only after its simulations pass numerical verification. Six open demonstrators implement 18 tasks from six engineering courses. In the eight tasks with quantitative cross-checks, every quantity met its tolerance at default settings (1\%, or 2\% for the finite-difference time-domain simulation) and agreed with a separate Python re-computation and a value-blinded MATLAB re-computation run by a colleague not involved in development; the checks also flagged under-resolved settings. In a perception survey, students (19 after post-hoc screening of 28 responses) reported that the pages linked equations with simulation, and 74\% preferred them to separate files, but usability was marginal (System Usability Scale 56.8). Twelve lecturers rated the approach as useful (item means 4.25--4.58) but were hesitant to adopt it; their median ratings on a 12-criterion capability rubric agreed moderately with the first author's ($\kappa_w=0.60$; individual median 0.31). The results show technical feasibility and preliminary positive perceptions; learning outcomes were not measured.
item.dc:creator: Xuan-Quy Dao, Ngoc-Bich Le, Xuan-Dung Phan, Le-Minh Nguyen

item.title: Terms of Care: Designing for Participation in Data Governance by Disability Communities
item.description: arXiv:2611.15720v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Improving disability representation in AI-generated media requires community-specific datasets, yet openly sharing such data can expose communities to misuse, decontextualization, and exploitation. We examine how disability communities can participate in dataset governance through context-sensitive licensing. Working with three disability advocacy organizations, we conducted semi-structured interviews, an educational webinar and modular license activity to promote community participation in data stewardship. Our findings show that governance in these high-context communities relies on organizational memory (especially situated harms); both formal authority and informal relational practices; communication; and resulting trust. The modular license activity made organizational data choices more accessible and values-led, allowing communities to adapt Creative Commons clauses to express permitted uses, sector-specific restrictions, safeguarding requirements, and commitments to respectful representation. Yet, concerns remain about monitoring and enforcing appropriate data use. We contribute (1) an empirical account of governance tensions, (2) a practical modular approach, and (3) design implications for AI data platforms that support relational, context-sensitive governance beyond standardized, one-size-fits-all frameworks.
item.dc:creator: Madiha Zahrah Choksi, Reeda Shimaz Huda, Rita Faia Marques, Anja Thieme, Cecily Morrison

item.title: Right Advice, Wrong Reasons: How Decision and Reasoning Alignment Shape Reliance on AI Advisors
item.description: arXiv:2611.15732v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When people seek advice from AI on social situations, the system may recommend a decision they fully agree with but justify it through reasoning they disagree with. Conversely, it may offer reasoning they agree with, and yet reach a decision they reject. We distinguish decision alignment, whether an advisor recommends the option favored by a user's measured values, from reason alignment, whether its stated reasons align with the user's values. In this work, we ask how these two forms of alignment shape people's preferences for AI advisors and their willingness to use them in different roles. We conducted a within-subjects study (N=121) in which participants evaluated three AI advisors varying in decision and reason alignment across eight everyday moral dilemmas. Participants then chose which advisors they would consult, allow to draft messages for review, or allow to act on their behalf in new tasks. When seeking advice, participants most often preferred an advisor that reasoned through their prioritized values while recommending the opposing decision (40%). However, when participants had to pick advisors for new tasks, their preferences shifted toward advisors that also recommended decisions aligned with their values, rather than those that only shared their reasons. Also, as participants considered tasks that gave AI advisors greater autonomy, they became more likely to opt out of using any advisor, from 12% when consulting to 38% when allowing an advisor to act on their behalf. Our findings suggest that decision and reason alignment shape advisor preferences differently across contexts of AI use, and that alignment with a user's values does not necessarily imply willingness to delegate.
item.dc:creator: Eunkyu Park, Vasudha Varadarajan, Wesley Hanwen Deng, Anisha Reddy, Gunhee Kim, Motahhare Eslami, Jana Schaich Borg, Maarten Sap

item.title: Trained on What Screen Readers Cannot Read: Accessibility Debt in the GUI Corpora Behind Computer-Use Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.16107v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computer-use agents learn to operate mobile interfaces from corpora of captured screens and accessibility trees. The same trees are what a screen reader consumes, so an agent trained on them inherits whatever labelling gaps the underlying applications carry. This paper measures one of those gaps, content-description coverage, in two Android corpora: Rico, collected in 2017, and AndroidControl, collected in 2024. Across 17,373,614 interface elements, 17.74% of the Rico elements that need a content description under our coding rule carry one, against 57.27% in AndroidControl. The difference of 39.5 percentage points holds under five alternative coding rules and when whole apps are resampled. It describes two datasets that also differ in app selection, capture method and platform version; it does not measure change over time. Input controls are the least labelled role in both corpora (2.20% and 27.21%, or 30.99% in AndroidControl if hint text counts as a name). Descriptions in the older corpus are also five times more likely to be placeholders (10.25% against 1.95%), so the difference is not an artefact of developers typing filler. Resolving 26,205 task actions to the elements they touched shows that, among tappable graphics with no text, demonstrations operate elements described 9.0 points more often than the others on the screens they visit, about 3.5 points of it from the choice of element within a screen. That is a selection effect inside the benchmark. A two-coder reliability check (kappa = 0.91 and 0.96) and the full pipeline accompany the paper.
item.dc:creator: Obada Kraishan, Kulsawasd Jitkajornwanich

item.title: How Do People Debug Complex SQL Queries With LLMs? A Qualitative Study
item.description: arXiv:2611.16108v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While LLMs are increasingly used in various contexts, we lack a fundamental understanding of how they impact SQL query debugging. In response, we conducted a user study with 16 participants of varying SQL expertise, examining how they debug complex SQL queries with and without LLM support. Initial benchmarking indicated that our selected models are already capable SQL debuggers. Qualitative analyses of our study data revealed that while participants trusted the LLM, they varied widely in how and whether they delegated debugging tasks to the LLMs, which we characterized through a new three-state model of participants' SQL reasoning processes. Additionally, participants enforced specific collaborative roles for the LLM such as TA or sounding board, which participants controlled by withholding context from the LLM. These findings suggest that LLM-based tools could enable preset role selection, broader context management, and flexible automation features, including low automation options, to support SQL debugging moving forward.
item.dc:creator: Nicole Sullivan, Ella Cao, Leilani Battle, Magdalena Balazinska

item.title: MRxD: A Usage-Pattern Framework for Mixed-Reality Cross-Device Interaction
item.description: arXiv:2611.16171v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mixed reality (MR) cross-device experiences often combine MR headsets with non-immersive devices such as laptops, tablets, and phones. Yet such cross-device design remains challenging because users must coordinate workflows across heterogeneous devices with different roles. This motivates our focus on usage patterns: recurrent ways in which people distribute and coordinate work across devices. Through a systematic analysis of 238 MR cross-device papers, we developed MRxD, a usage-pattern framework organized around three dimensions: user attention, task relatedness, and cognitive symmetry. Using these dimensions, we identified six usage patterns and synthesized the design strategies commonly used within each pattern. We further investigated the framework's application in design practice through a workshop (n=6) and the results suggest that MRxD can guide pattern-based design exploration and identify blind spots. We further discuss how usage patterns may shift or combine, and outline research gaps and design implications for future MR cross-device systems.
item.dc:creator: Yang Zhan, Yuxuan Huang, Yuchen Cai, Yichen Andy Yu, Xiaoran Yang, Ye Yuan, Qiao Jin

item.title: "We Are the Dirty Hands": Reimagining an Ambient Intelligence Care System with Professional Caregivers
item.description: arXiv:2611.16198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While ambient assisted living (AAL) sensing systems offer promise for aging in place, their impacts on professional caregivers are overlooked. We conducted two collective speculation workshops (N=24) with personal health aides (PHAs, n=18) and certified nursing assistants (CNAs, n=6) to examine the ethical implications and value tensions of a care system with ambient intelligence (CSAI), our conceptualization of an AAL. Participants anticipated different implications across care roles and settings. PHAs anticipated additional responsibilities from CSAI, including learning how it operates and supporting older adults in its use. CNAs, who had greater access to workplace resources and protections, similarly noted that CSAI could create additional work. Participants also identified tensions around visibility, as sensing could support caregivers by documenting difficult working conditions while simultaneously making their behavior more vulnerable to misinterpretation. Through their modifications and surfaced discussions, we propose design guidelines for AAL systems, such as integrating context-aware sensing.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Green, Jane L. E, Sneha Jain, Parker Ruth, Matthew J\"orke, Sarah L. Billington, James Landay, Andrea Cuadra

item.title: Agentic Dashboards: A New Design Paradigm for Visual Analytics
item.description: arXiv:2611.16245v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Visual analytics systems traditionally combine analytical methods and interactive visualizations into a fixed application specified at the design phase. Coding agents offer a flexible approach: experts could conduct analysis through natural-language instructions. We envision an agentic dashboard as a persistent visual analytics workspace where an agent makes decisions about analytical methods, views, and their coordination within a designer-defined decision space. This approach shifts part of the visualization designer's role from engineering a fixed interface to defining the decisions an agent may make at runtime. We illustrate how such a dashboard could operate with current capabilities and propose criteria for evaluating its behavior and potential failures. As analytical workflows become more fluid and agent-mediated, visualization can help experts maintain awareness, coordinate with agents, and exercise judgment.
item.dc:creator: Sam Yu-Te Lee, Yun-Hsin Kuo, Kwan-Liu Ma

item.title: RiskLens: Human-Informed Incident Transfer for AI Risk Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2611.16287v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI capabilities advance, early-stage teams need better ways to judge whether historical incidents transfer to new products, demanding support beyond static risk checklists or one-off ideation tools. We present RiskLens, a human-AI workflow with an interactive system built around a live crawl, refreshable ranker, and extensible, human-informed schema. RiskLens analyzes 2,034 AI incidents and 10,443 AI products to rank transferable incidents using a feature schema spanning technical, operational, and user-facing attributes and supports an interface that presents ranked incident evidence, generated scenarios, risk metrics, and mitigation suggestions. In a study with 21 AI-familiar participants, users surfaced evaluation criteria that we added as 13 human-informed dimensions, including harm categories, failure mechanisms, and vulnerable groups. The feature-based model outperformed a generic baseline with an 86.2% win rate, and remained stable on a twenty-month future holdout; after human-informed schema expansion, the updated model outperformed the same baseline on 91.4% of pairs.
item.dc:creator: Yiliu Tang, Hangyue Zhang, Yun Huang

item.title: A Serious Game for Training Civil Participation in Flood Crisis Management
item.description: arXiv:2611.16446v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Floods are among the most frequent and destructive natural disasters, requiring citizens to make critical decisions under rapidly changing conditions. Most serious games related to flooding emphasize awareness, preparedness, and education in flood management, but there is still a research gap on how to train citizens to act under pressure, uncertainty, and stress. In this paper, we position Virtual Reality (VR) serious games as a promising approach to addressing this gap by providing experiential and immersive training opportunities for citizens. We propose a conceptual VR serious game that enables participants to experience realistic flood scenarios, practice decision-making, rehearse appropriate response behaviors, and develop response-related skills in a safe and controlled environment. In addition, we suggest a research agenda and an evaluation framework focused on flood risk awareness, response capabilities, and stress-related outcomes. The framework thoughtfully integrates subjective, objective, and physiological measures to assess the effectiveness of immersive flood-response training. Finally, we present design, methodological, ethical, and user-experience considerations in VR-based disaster training, and outline future research directions for the development and evaluation of immersive serious games for flood emergency response. The present study aims to contribute to the growing intersection of serious games, extended reality, and disaster risk reduction by establishing citizen-centered response training as a significant yet under-researched field.
item.dc:creator: Solmaz Goodarzi, Arseni Ivanov, David Maruscs\'ak, Diana Quit\'eria Sousa

item.title: Language Learning through Immersive Multi-User Gamification
item.description: arXiv:2611.16594v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose an immersive virtual-reality game designed to enable multi-user, multi-language learning during co-play. We hypothesize that our method will be more engaging, leading to better rhythm, pronunciation, memorization, and speaking confidence. We implement the experience as a fantasy role-playing game by introducing vocabulary and phrases to the user as spells to learn. Players then cast more efficient spells depending on their language skills. For evaluation, we compare the game to a single-user baseline that replicates traditional language learning in a non-immersive setting. We measure short- and long-term retention of vocabulary and phrases, as well as scoring rhythm and pronunciation. Furthermore, we collect user data on engagement and mental workload.
item.dc:creator: Rosalina Ribeiro Silva, Zichen Feng, Rikard Olajos, Tim Rolff

item.title: People prefer AI to human advice in multi-turn conversations but neither changes incentivised behaviour
item.description: arXiv:2611.16667v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: People increasingly ask AI chatbots for advice, yet large language models (LLMs) are sycophantic, overconfident, and can amplify human cognitive biases. In this article, we investigate how people perceive advice from humans versus LLMs and whether AI advice reshapes incentive-compatible donation decisions. Using Carrier, a new experimental platform, we designed an experiment where participants made a donation decision after discussing it with an AI chatbot advisor, another human, or receiving no advice. Participants judged LLM advisors to be significantly more rational, trustworthy, convincing, and sycophantic than human advisors. Analysis of chatlogs showed that LLMs were more engaged than human advisors: they shared more facts and more often stated their opinion and justified their recommendations. Despite this, donation decisions did not vary across conditions.
item.dc:creator: Maximilian Maier, Tsz Kwan Emmy Wong, Jiahao Eric Yang, Falk Lieder, Vanessa Cheung

item.title: It Was Better Not to Know: Digital Recognition, Family Authority, and Postpartum Mental Health in Bangladesh
item.description: arXiv:2611.16993v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Postpartum mental distress affects roughly one in five mothers in low- and lower-middle-income countries, yet recognition and support remain limited where formal mental-health care is scarce, and family relationships govern health decisions. We report a five-month interview study with 20 mothers in urban, urban slum, and rural Bangladesh who had given birth within the previous two years. Mothers encountered the concept of postpartum depression incidentally, through Facebook and YouTube recommendations rather than deliberate search or clinical guidance, and then used these platforms for private sensemaking without disclosing. Recognition, however, rarely traveled beyond the self: mothers could identify their distress while families dismissed it, leaving them with knowledge but no authority to act. Participants sought validation as a precondition for support and described recovery as relational rather than clinical or digital. We argue that postpartum technologies should engage partners, families, and community health workers rather than placing recognition solely on mothers.
item.dc:creator: Shajnin Haque Aishy, Sabbir Bin Abdul Latif, Md. Golam Zel A Husna, Jannatun Noor

item.title: DiffSSMEye: Conditional High-Frequency Eye Movement Synthesis with Structured State-Space Diffusion
item.description: arXiv:2611.17013v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Synthesizing high-frequency eye movements requires preserving long-range temporal dependencies and subject-specific oculomotor dynamics. However, methods based on generative adversarial networks (GANs) and variational autoencoders (VAEs) can struggle to preserve these characteristics simultaneously. We introduce DiffSSMEye, a conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model with bidirectional Structured State Space Sequence (S4) layers for generating five-second gaze-velocity sequences at 1,000 Hz. Generation is conditioned on a coarse gaze reference, user identity, and task, where identity and task embeddings are incorporated through feature-wise linear modulation. Identity-preservation, multi-resolution spectral, and integrated-drift losses complement noise prediction to constrain biometric consistency, frequency structure, and displacement error. Subject-disjoint evaluation on GazeBase across seven tasks yields mean real--synthetic embedding cosine similarities of 0.91--0.95. DiffSSMEye also achieves the lowest median spatial errors among these baselines for horizontal and random saccade tasks. These results demonstrate improved spatial accuracy and biometric feature consistency for subject-specific gaze synthesis.
item.dc:creator: Kamrul Hasan, Mehedi Hasan Raju, Oleg V. Komogortsev

item.title: Exploring Socially Acceptable 3D Feedback Design for Inclusive Small-Group Conversation
item.description: arXiv:2611.17018v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prior research has shown that providing feedback on group dynamics can improve the quality of small-group conversations. However, publicly delivered feedback that targets specific individuals may reduce social acceptability due to negative experiences such as social pressure, embarrassment, and resistance. This work investigates how public feedback can be designed to remain socially acceptable while maintaining its effectiveness in XR-based small-group conversations. Informed by social science and HCI literature, we identified three design strategies (incorporate humor, reduce social attention, and use indirectness) and proposed a set of metaphor- and agent-based 3D feedback probes. We then conducted a two-phase study: (1) an online survey with 50 participants to examine how such feedback designs are perceived under public and private delivery, and (2) follow-up interviews with 14 participants who completed the survey to better understand their interpretations and elicit additional insights. Results show that metaphor- and agent-based feedback can reduce social discomfort while maintaining effectiveness. Interview findings further highlighted the role of three strategies in making feedback easier to accept, while requiring careful balance. We also discussed design implications for creating socially acceptable 3D feedback to support inclusive small-group conversations in XR.
item.dc:creator: Qianjie Wei, Yifan Li, Zhen Bai

item.title: Neural Representations as New Modes of Interactivity
item.description: arXiv:2611.17058v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Human-AI interaction today runs almost entirely through prompts and outputs, keeping AI systems opaque to general users. We introduce Neural Representation Interaction (NRI), a paradigm that treats the internal representations of neural networks as an interaction material people can inspect, steer, and edit. Situating NRI alongside graphical, tangible, and bio-computer interaction, we argue that the concepts and algorithms models encode internally offer representational affordances for richer human-AI interaction. We synthesize actionable mechanistic interpretability methods and, drawing on General Morphological Analysis, construct a design space spanning Interaction, Target, Referent, and Purpose. Mapping existing interfaces onto this space reveals that most serve expert auditors, while few support lay users. We then present speculative applications in education, personal user modeling, and hiring audits, and discuss design principles, limitations, and sociotechnical risks. NRI offers HCI researchers abstractions for designing interactions that work with AI computation rather than only through its inputs and outputs.
item.dc:creator: Stanley Huang, Anthony Baez, Catherine Yeh, Pat Pataranutaporn

item.title: A Compact xDAWN-Guided Spatio-Temporal Network with Filter-Bank Convolution for P300 Detection
item.description: arXiv:2611.17101v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: P300-based brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) enable communication by decoding stimulus-evoked EEG responses into character selections without requiring voluntary motor output. Reliable P300 detection remains difficult because of low response amplitude and signal-to-noise ratio, while practical spellers require accurate character selection with few stimulus repetitions and low computational cost. We propose a compact deep learning architecture that combines xDAWN spatial filtering for event-related potential enhancement and dimensionality reduction, a fixed frequency-selective filter bank, and convolutional feature learning for spatio-temporal EEG decoding. Depthwise-separable convolutions and progressive average pooling reduce computational complexity while retaining discriminative temporal information. The resulting target/non-target classifier contains only 5,100 trainable parameters. We evaluated the model on two public benchmarks, BCI Competition II Dataset IIb and BCI Competition III Dataset II, and compared it with established P300 decoding methods across different numbers of stimulus repetitions. The model achieved an information transfer rate of 17.8 bits/min with two repetitions on BCI Competition III and 40.5 bits/min on BCI Competition II, demonstrating a favorable accuracy-speed trade-off. These results suggest that combining domain-informed spatial and spectral priors with compact neural networks can support efficient P300 decoding for EEG-based BCI communication.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Mahdi Habibi Bina, Mohammad Reza Daliri

item.title: Known Good, Known Bad: A Ground-Truth Calibration Protocol for AI Judgment in Science
item.description: arXiv:2611.11673v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Scientific use of generative AI requires evaluation against cases with independently checkable answers. We present a ground truth calibration protocol that compares a verified reference case with reference deviant variants through neutral evaluation, an authority framed recheck, and a line by line audit. Human adjudication distinguishes deviation detection, premise accommodation, unsupported doubt, and correctness of the resulting calculation. An instructor generated organic chemistry demonstration comprises six conversations and 18 responses from an unidentified backend served through the free logged out ChatGPT interface in July 2026. Neutral evaluation detected three of five intended deviations. Both initial misses, involving oxidant stoichiometry and experimental scale, were detected at the authority framed second turn; all five detections persisted at the third turn audit. The fixed sequence supports a descriptive account of recovery across turns. In the scale case, the model initially produced a locally coherent peroxide limited yield. After recognizing the unit problem, it incorrectly retained that limiting reagent conclusion for the corrected scale. Detection and numerical repair therefore require separate assessment. The verified reference attracted speculative concerns while retaining its correct yield calculation. The protocol connects documentary verification of scientific claims and citations with empirical verification of laboratory interpretations. It supplies inspectable transcripts, reference calculations, behavior codes, and a reusable calibration architecture for AI literacy instruction. The pilot demonstrates the protocol's measures in one case family; replicated model evaluation and learner assessment are the next validation steps.
item.dc:creator: Olga Lavinda

item.title: Can I join you? Extended Social Force Based Model with Predictive Control and Barrier Functions for Humanoid Group Repositioning Amidst Obstacles
item.description: arXiv:2611.14853v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As social and service robots increasingly share interaction spaces in public, they may form groups while coordinating tasks or interacting with humans. Initial group formation alone is insufficient in dynamic settings, because it can be disrupted when a person or another agent joins, leaves, or passes through the group. Although group dynamics and repositioning have been widely studied in swarm robotics and virtual-agent settings, little attention has been given to socially appropriate repositioning behaviors in groups of humanoid robots. Existing social-force-based approaches provide a useful foundation for group behavior, but they have limited obstacle handling, and can produce unsafe behavior as environmental complexity increases. We propose a novel framework that modulates traditional Social Force, guided by Model Predictive Control (MPC) to plan ahead, bounded by Control Barrier Functions (CBF) to increase safety for robot groups repositioning behaviors. This approach aims to produce safer and socially aware group repositioning behaviors under various group formation disturbance. We evaluate the method in simulation through an ablation study and an online user study. The results show that our proposed method can produce smoother and safer repositioning behaviors in complex environments while preserving social appropriateness.
item.dc:creator: Chuxuan Zhang, Niloofar Jahanshahi, Yasaman Etesam, Mo Chen, Angelica Lim

item.title: Calibrate, Don't Retrain: Decomposing the Value of Annotator Disagreement in Cyberbullying Severity
item.description: arXiv:2611.15010v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine learning models are often trained on labeled data produced by multiple human annotators. When those annotators disagree, their labels are commonly collapsed into a single majority vote, which discards information about the underlying disagreement. We examine the cost of this practice for cyberbullying severity, a subjective judgment on which annotators disagree heavily. In the corpus we study, all 5 annotators assigned the same severity label to only 4.1% of comments. Turning 5 judgments into one label hides this disagreement and obscures how much the annotators differed in their assessments. In this paper, we ask whether a model can preserve this information by predicting the distribution of annotator judgments instead of a single majority label. We find 3 main results. First, accuracy against the majority label cannot tell competent models apart: 2 models with similar accuracy can differ greatly in how well they match the distribution of annotator judgments. Second, predicting the full distribution requires little extra effort. Calibrating an existing model, which adjusts its output probabilities after training, captures most of the improvement without retraining, across 3 datasets covering severity, abuse, and irony, while training on label distributions adds a small further gain. Third, we examine a dataset that includes annotator demographics, where a single shared model has one advantage and one limit. The advantage is that a model predicting the distribution of judgments matches each demographic group's judgments significantly better than a model trained on majority labels, so both groups gain. The limit is that it does not narrow the gap in performance between the groups, because one shared model cannot encode which group is right on a given comment. Preserving annotator disagreement is therefore a low-cost step toward fairer moderation, though not a complete one.
item.dc:creator: Arslan Bisharat, Katelyn Skees, Manuel Sandoval Madrigal, Mujtaba Nazari, Ayaan Khan, Deborah L. Hall, Mohammed Abuhamad, Yasin N. Silva

item.title: Estimating Image Creativity
item.description: arXiv:2611.15044v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: What makes an image creative? Although this may seem like a highly subjective decision, research in psychology suggests that creativity may be based on a set of fundamental creativity dimensions such as novelty, surprise, and arousal. A deeper understanding of image creativity can benefit both research and practical applications. Exploring how human viewers use creativity dimensions to evaluate image creativity may allow us to predict a target image's human-rated creativity automatically. We present a novel framework to estimate the perceived creativity of an image by: (1) predicting the strengths of an image's novelty, surprise, and arousal creativity dimensions, and (2) combining the creativity dimension strengths to estimate an image creativity score. Controlled human-subject experiments were conducted on Amazon Mechanical Turk to collect data to train supervised machine learning models to estimate an image's strengths on the three creativity dimensions. A final machine learning model takes the predicted dimension strengths as input to produce an estimated image creativity score. Results showed that our estimated creativity scores are statistically equivalent to human ratings of creativity for the images we tested. The novel contributions of our research are: (1) identification and validation of three psychological creativity dimensions used to estimate image creativity; (2) supervised machine learning models to automatically estimate novelty, surprise, and arousal strengths for an input image; (3) a supervised machine learning model to predict a creativity score from novelty, surprise, and arousal strengths for an input image, and (4) experimental methods to confirm the accuracy, advantages, and limitations of our approach.
item.dc:creator: Nisan Chhetri, Christopher G. Healey, Sina Baghbanijam

item.title: Computational Raga Recognition: A Theory-Driven Approach
item.description: arXiv:2611.15242v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Raga recognition in Hindustani classical music is difficult because a raga is not defined only by the notes used in it. Its identity also depends on the way notes are emphasized, the movement between notes and characteristic phrases. In this work, we develop a computational approach to analyse these characteristics directly from audio recordings. The method uses pitch extracted from recordings and represents it using a 44-position note framework based on the 22-shruti system. From this representation, Raga features based on the Indian classical musicology are extracted.Each feature is compared with a reference representation of the raga and the resulting scores are combined to obtain an overall similarity score. The method is first studied using Raga Yaman and is then tested on recordings of other ragas. The computational results are also compared with the theoretical description of Yaman to identify which raga characteristics are captured well and where the method has limitations.
item.dc:creator: Janay Sukheja, Shailaja D. Sharma

item.title: Read and Ignore: What Self-Directed LLM Agents Do in Public Service Scenarios
item.description: arXiv:2611.15460v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Underspecified instructions leave LLM agents to decide what to do. In public services, staff write these instructions, but the agent's decisions affect residents, patients, and students. We build four expert-validated public-service scenarios with records and decision levers that can be checked in the files, collect $2{,}400$ trajectories from ten LLMs under four prompt conditions, and compare them with $1{,}000$ runs in a context-free sandbox. Agents read the records in $96.9\%$ of open-ended runs and produce an artifact or a self-chosen task in $18.7\%$; with an explicit task, $86.0\%$ produce. Domain context does not change how many runs produce ($18.7\%$ vs.\ $16.0\%$), and the production ranking of the models largely carries over (Spearman $0.79$), while the ranking by whether a model reads the records does not ($0.19$). Context cuts boundary-probing turns per run by $60\%$, and some artifacts contradict the records. We contribute a test that a public-service institution can run on its own records before procurement; its rule-based taxonomy needs no labeled data, and scenarios, code, and trajectories are released.
item.dc:creator: Diana Kozachek, Kinjalk Srivastava

item.title: What You See Is (Not) What You Got: The Human Factor in PDF Signature Verification
item.description: arXiv:2611.15472v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Signed PDF documents have legally binding value under frameworks such as the EU's eIDAS regulation. In this work, we present Genuine PDF Forgeries, a novel attack class that focuses on human factors in signature validation. Our attacks target the disconnect between cryptographically verifiable signer certificates and human-visible signature blocks embedded in documents. We analyze our attacks against 23 PDF viewers and validation tools across desktop platforms and the web. We find that nine of the 13 viewers that automatically report signature validity hide authenticated signer information behind additional user interaction. We then evaluate the attack in twin deception-based online studies with 584 EU-based participants. To further validate the impact, we perform a highly tailored real-world attack study with six trials within two privacy-sensitive organizations. Five of six organizational trials accepted requests authenticated using the forged visual identity. In the online studies (total n=584), the most effective attack variant deceives 71.9% of eligible participants on first impression, and 57.3% continue to be deceived even after we prompt for additional introspection. We derive viewer-side countermeasures and prototype a safeguard that overlays the untrusted signature block with signer information obtained from the validated certificate. Our results show that boolean validity indicators, not associated with the authenticated signer identity, are insufficient in practice.
item.dc:creator: Jakob Heher, Emanuel Pichler, Stefan More

item.title: Human-Likeness and Conversational Preference Diverge for Synthesized Agent Speech in Customer-Service Calls
item.description: arXiv:2611.16051v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Listeners can judge an agent's speech on how human it sounds (human-likeness) and on how much they would want to talk to it (conversational preference). Listening tests rarely ask about conversational preference, so the relation between the two judgments is unclear. We compared them in paired-choice tests on 120 turns that actors improvised as customer-service representatives. On each trial, two agents spoke the same turn. In Study 1, both agents came from six commercial text-to-speech systems, each with eight voices. In Study 2, one was the actor's original recording and the other a system. Some systems ranked higher on human-likeness, and others on conversational preference. Listeners chose systems over actors in 19% of human-likeness trials but 36% of conversational preference trials (and 49% for the most preferred system). On both judgments, variation among a system's voices was about three-quarters of that between systems. Of three automatic naturalness scores, two predicted lower human-likeness, and none predicted conversational preference. In this setting, listeners tended to favor faster speech and fewer pauses between clauses on both judgments, and more pitch variation for conversational preference. Thus, measuring only human-likeness or testing one voice per system can misjudge which agents listeners would rather talk to.
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey M. Girard, Antony D'Avirro, Jason Z. Zheng, Jacqueline R. Vertino, Benjamin Peloquin

item.title: Between Niti and Nyaya: A Society-Centered Framework for AI Governance
item.description: arXiv:2611.16173v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Governments are making decisions about AI before they can measure its public effects, and those decisions determine whether a person can learn that AI influenced an outcome, challenge it, and see it corrected. Research has documented what AI governance produces: principles, strategies, registers, and audits. However, we lack shared language for understanding AI policy while it is still being made. We introduce the Society-Centered AI Governance Framework, which gives policymakers, researchers, and the public a way to assess instruments in any jurisdiction by whether a person can get notice, challenge a decision, and see it corrected. It reads a jurisdiction's instruments together by date and binding status, separates an agency duty from a right a person can invoke, and traces which later instrument must enforce each commitment. We evaluated it in North Carolina using interviews with nine AI Leadership Council members, conducted before and after the state's 2026 AI roadmap, and a provision-level reading, with human-reviewed model-assisted coding, of 49 AI governance documents from 19 states. For the state's own AI systems, we find visibility-first governance: visibility duties are in effect, notice exists as an agency duty with no right a person can invoke, and AI-specific challenge and correction remain advisory. The roadmap assigns owners and dates to the missing protections, so the gaps are documented but not yet closed. Recent federal preemption proposals focus on AI development, so recourse for a state's own systems is likely to remain a state decision. We identify "legitimacy before protection" as a testable risk of visibility-first governance and name the milestones that would test it. More broadly, judging AI policy by who can act on what it makes visible lets the field assess recourse while policy is still forming, before harm occurs.
item.dc:creator: Snehalkumar `Neil' S. Gaikwad, Punya Aragula, Shiva Kruthi Palpanoori, Pratik Patekar

item.title: Rasoi: Visual Diffs for Evaluating Structural Changes Made by Coding Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.16293v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coding agents let developers modify software rapidly through natural language. However, as agents take on larger changes, developers can lose track of how the codebase is evolving. These edits may look correct on the surface while restructuring the system in unexpected ways: duplicating logic, changing modules outside the requested scope, removing functionality developers meant to keep, or introducing architectural drift. We investigate how visual diffs can help developers understand and evaluate the structural changes that coding agents make. We present Rasoi, a design probe that maps how a codebase's architecture evolves after each agent-made edit, letting developers inspect which architectural elements and relationships were added, modified, or removed across multiple levels of abstraction. We deployed Rasoi in a week-long study with 12 developers working on their own codebases across varied technical domains. We found that visual diffs helped developers see whether changes stayed within scope, notice unexpected restructuring, and understand how modified parts related to the system as a whole. Our findings suggest that the value of oversight tools for coding agents lies less in making developers trust the agent and more in helping developers feel confident in their own evaluation of agent-made changes. We discuss implications for visual tools that support code comprehension and human oversight in AI-assisted software development.
item.dc:creator: Riya Sahni, Aryan Kaul, Anushka Bhatnagar, Xuanming Zhang, Vivian Liu, Reya Vir, Lydia B. Chilton

item.title: Robots That Talk Too Much and Don't Listen Enough
item.description: arXiv:2611.16473v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Until recently, the biggest obstacles to natural spoken interaction with social robots were speech recognition errors and turn-taking failures. Advances in speech recognition have enabled much better spoken interaction, but turn-taking failures and other misunderstandings continue to be far too prevalent. This short paper looks back at earlier methods for improving speech recognition and turn-taking in interaction with social robots, and then looks at what can be done today, arguing that multimodal bidirectional streaming is needed to reduce the frequency of turn-taking failures.
item.dc:creator: Graham Wilcock, Kristiina Jokinen

item.title: A Dual-Branch Graph and Convolutional Network for Interpretable Movement EEG Classification
item.description: arXiv:2611.16609v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Decoding upper-limb movements from scalp electroencephalography (EEG) is an important problem for brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), but many deep learning models provide limited insight into the brain regions underlying their predictions. We propose a two-branch architecture that combines an LGGNet-inspired local-global graph branch with an EEGNet-style convolutional branch for movement-versus-rest classification. The graph branch groups 61 EEG electrodes into anatomically informed regions and learns their spatial relationships, providing a direct representation of the regions emphasized by the model. We evaluate the proposed architecture using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation on the Ofner upper-limb movement dataset. The model achieves a mean F1-score of 0.74 +/- 0.06 across subjects. Beyond classification performance, we analyze the learned graph structure to identify the regions with the strongest connectivity. Across all held-out subjects, the highest connectivity is consistently observed in the Parietal Left Low region, corresponding to electrodes P1 and P3. This region is opposite to the performed right-arm movements and lies within the posterior parietal area previously associated with upper-limb movement processing. These results show that incorporating a region-based graph into the decoder can provide an anatomically interpretable representation while maintaining effective movement classification, offering a practical approach toward more transparent EEG-based BCIs.
item.dc:creator: Maryam Ostadsharif Memar, Behzad Nazari

item.title: A Connectionless Interaction Model for Network Spatial Proximity Services
item.description: arXiv:2611.16737v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, we present a connectionless interaction model for network spatial proximity services. In the network spatial proximity model, the reception of an identification or discovery frame of a nearby wireless node confirms proximity and delivers content at the same time. Current Bluetooth and Wi-Fi specifications and mobile platforms extend this one-way announcement with responses, addressed messages, scheduled group exchange, and relaying, which still do not require a connection. The proposed model describes such interaction independently of a concrete wireless technology. It is based on the roles of nearby nodes, the proximity message as the unit of interaction, twelve pattern properties, and six interaction patterns: announcement, mutual announcement, query-response, addressed exchange, scheduled group exchange, and relay. An exit rule defines when a service should move to a connection-based channel. We analyze how the patterns can be implemented on Android and iOS smartphones through native mechanisms, substitution, composition, embedded bridges, or a step-up to a connection, and we propose a pattern selection method for developers. The model generalizes the earlier network spatial proximity model and refines the interaction primitives of the proximity core. It is illustrated by existing services and systems and supported by published measurements and first-order estimates.
item.dc:creator: Artem Makarov, Dmitry Namiot

item.title: Beyond Curiosity: Habit and Organizational Learning Capability as Predictors of Shadow AI
item.description: arXiv:2611.16931v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative AI has entered the workplace faster than organizations can govern it. A large share of employees now use AI tools their employer has not sanctioned, and many actively conceal that use, but the psychology of this covert technology behavior remains poorly understood. A common assumption, in popular accounts and early commentary, treats unauthorized (shadow) AI use as curiosity-driven exploration by adventurous individuals. We test this against a competing account grounded in the psychology of habitual technology use, in which automaticity rather than exploratory disposition sustains the behavior. Using survey data from 510 employed generative AI users across multiple countries, we adjudicated among individual and contextual predictors (workplace curiosity, habit, technology-acceptance beliefs, and organizational learning capability) with hierarchical regression, relative weights analysis with bootstrap confidence intervals, and full-subset dominance analysis. Habit was the strongest predictor, accounting for 28.3% of explained variance, and completely dominated joyous exploration, the curiosity dimension most aligned with the exploration account, across all 512 possible predictor subsets. Joyous exploration contributed 3.4% (95% CI [1.6, 7.4]) and fell to nonsignificance once use behavior and habit were modeled. Learning-supportive organizational conditions accounted for a further 24.1% and operated additively rather than by moderating dispositions. Parallel models decomposing the outcome showed the same dominance pattern for unauthorized use and concealment, and perceived social support for AI use was protective specifically against concealment. These findings reframe shadow AI as a habit-and-environment phenomenon rather than an individual-exploration phenomenon. The cross-sectional design means causal claims are exploratory.
item.dc:creator: Nolan Lovett, Mohan Yang

item.title: HarmonICA: Quasi-Time-Invariant ICA for Motor Unit Decomposition during Dynamic Contractions
item.description: arXiv:2406.19581v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Decomposing surface electromyography (EMG) into the spike trains of individual motor neurons is a long-standing inverse problem and a key step toward motor-neuron-driven neural interfaces such as prosthetics and exoskeletons. The standard approach, independent component analysis (ICA) of the multichannel signal, assumes that the mixing from neurons to electrodes is stationary in time. This assumption fails during movement, when volume-conductor deformation makes the mixing time-varying, and current decomposition algorithms are correspondingly restricted to isometric contractions. We introduce HarmonICA, a quasi-time-invariant ICA formulation in which a static linear separator is preceded by a learned, low-rank, time-varying invertible transformation. The separator is trained with an independence loss on the uncompensated projection, and the transformation with a stationarity loss on the recovered source. Gradients are not shared between the two, so source extraction remains a classical linear-ICA problem while non-stationary distortion is absorbed by the transformation. The closed-form inverse of the transformation enables per-spike subtraction with a time-varying template during sequential peel-off. On a public simulated benchmark of dynamic high-density EMG with ground-truth spike trains, the method outperforms five adaptive ICA baselines at every recall threshold, recovering more units at a higher accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Kenneth Clarke, Dimitrios Halatsis, Agnese Grison, Irene Mendez Guerra, Noura Ezaz-Nikpay, Pranav Mamidanna, Shihan Ma, Silvia Muceli, Dario Farina

item.title: Tracer: A Forensic Framework for Detecting Fraudulent Speedruns from Game Replays
item.description: arXiv:2509.10848v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Speedrun, a practice of completing a game as quickly as possible, has fostered vibrant communities driven by creativity, competition, and mastery of game mechanics and motor skills. However, this contest also attracts malicious actors as financial incentives come into play. As media and software manipulation techniques advance - such as spliced footage, modified game software and live stream with staged setups - forged speedruns have become increasingly difficult to detect. Volunteer-driven communities invest significant effort to verify submissions, yet the process remains slow, inconsistent, and reliant on informal expertise. In high-profile cases, fraudulent runs have gone undetected for years, allowing perpetrators to gain fame and financial benefits through monetised viewership, sponsorships, donations, and community bounties. To address this gap, we propose Tracer, Tamper Recognition via Analysis of Continuity and Events in game Runs, a modular framework for identifying artefacts of manipulation in speedrun submissions. Tracer provides structured guidelines across audiovisual, physical, and cyberspace dimensions, systematically documenting dispersed in-game knowledge and previously reported fraudulent cases to enhance verification efficiency.
item.dc:creator: Jaeung Franciskus Yoo, Huy Kang Kim

item.title: Gaze-controlled segmentation improves object recognition accuracy in simulated phosphene vision
item.description: arXiv:2509.19957v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Visual neuroprosthetics provide a simplified visual sense through cameras, computers, and implanted electrodes. A central challenge is deciding what to convey with the few phosphenes available. We asked whether letting the user's gaze select the object that is conveyed in full, rather than extracting edges across the whole scene, improves object recognition in simulated phosphene vision. We developed Gaze-Controlled Segmentation (GCS), in which the point of gaze prompts the Segment Anything Model and the selected object is rendered as a filled region over the scene's edges at reduced intensity. In simulated phosphene vision, eight participants performed an object search-and-localization task under GCS, edge detection, and normal-vision conditions. Both phosphene conditions were gaze-contingent, and data were analysed with Bayesian mixed-effects models. Relative to edge detection, GCS produced a modest but credible improvement in identification accuracy on target-present trials (+9.4 percentage points, 95% highest-density interval [+4.3, +14.2]). Gaze reached the target about as often under both methods, consistent with an advantage at the identification stage. GCS trials tended to be slower (+2.7 s, [-0.8, +6.6]), a difference that was not credible, and in exploratory analyses the advantage was largest for cylindrical objects and absent for round ones. Stated preferences leaned toward GCS on most usability criteria, though with eight participants these are individually consistent with chance. The comparison does not isolate the contribution of the segmentation itself. These findings illustrate the potential of gaze-driven, interactive scene representation for neuroprosthetic vision, while underscoring that the gain is modest, task-dependent, and established so far only in simulated phosphene vision with sighted observers, using phosphenes larger than current implants would produce.
item.dc:creator: Eleftherios Papadopoulos (Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition and Behaviour, Radboud University, Nijmegen, The Netherlands), Umut G\"u\c{c}l\"u (Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition and Behaviour, Radboud University, Nijmegen, The Netherlands), Ya\u{g}mur G\"u\c{c}l\"ut\"urk (Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition and Behaviour, Radboud University, Nijmegen, The Netherlands)

item.title: VizCopilot: Fostering Appropriate Reliance on Enterprise Chatbots with Context Visualization
item.description: arXiv:2510.11954v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Enterprise AI chatbots show promise in supporting knowledge workers in information synthesis tasks by retrieving context from large, heterogeneous databases before generating answers. However, when the retrieved context misaligns with user intentions, these chatbots often produce ``irrelevantly right'' responses that raise the risk of overreliance. To foster appropriate reliance, we need a different approach than asking users to verify chatbot outputs. We posit that human oversight and modification of the context retrieval process can improve the quality of chatbots' outputs and users' awareness, resulting in more appropriate reliance and higher accountability. In this work, we explore this approach through a Research-through-Design study using VizCopilot, a chatbot extended with corpus visualization techniques. Through a within-subject study comparing VizCopilot and a simplified pure-text chatbot, we evaluate the role of visualization in enterprise chatbots and surface future design opportunities for fostering appropriate reliance through context engineering. Our findings show that visualization not only helps users detect and correct misaligned context, but also enhances user agency and system transparency. At the same time, the study reveals limitations regarding verification support and trust in AI summaries. Based on these findings, we discuss how visualization can foster appropriate reliance, the associated design trade-offs, and our vision towards transparent and sustainable human-AI interaction.
item.dc:creator: Sam Yu-Te Lee, Jingya Chen, Albert Calzaretto, Richard Lee, Samir Passi, Alice Ferng, Mihaela Vorvoreanu

item.title: Individualized Algorithmic Advice as a Strategic Signal on Competitive Markets
item.description: arXiv:2511.09454v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As algorithms increasingly mediate competitive decision-making, their influence extends beyond individual outcomes to shaping strategic market dynamics. In our experiment, we examined how algorithmic advice affects human behavior in a classic economic game with a unique, non-collusive, and analytically traceable equilibrium. Participants (N = 129) played a Cournot quantity competition with equilibrium-aligned or strategically biased algorithmic recommendations. While individualized equilibrium advice supported stable convergence, collusively downward-biased advice led to sustained underproduction and supracompetitive profits - hallmarks of tacit collusion. Participants' quantities converged faster and more consistently toward individualized than collective equilibrium advice, potentially due to an objective quality advantage or greater perceived ownership of the former. These findings demonstrate that algorithmic advice can function as a strategic signal, shaping coordination even without explicit communication. The results echo real-world concerns about algorithmic collusion and underscore the need for careful design and oversight of algorithmic decision-support systems in competitive environments.
item.dc:creator: Tobias R. Rebholz, Maxwell Uphoff, Christian H. R. Bernges, Florian Scholten

item.title: Bridging GenAI policy and practice: Brief instruction improves learning-oriented prompting in an introductory programming course
item.description: arXiv:2602.16033v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is now commonplace in higher education, yet unguided use can harm learning. Universities have responded with policies asking students to use GenAI for learning, not solutions, but how to translate these policies into classroom instruction remains untested. Here we report a randomized controlled trial with a six-week, end-of-semester follow-up (N = 431) in an introductory programming course comparing four instructional approaches, from a two-sentence reminder (Condition 1) to a multi-step constructive task (Condition 4). We found: (1) all four approaches produced learning-oriented prompting gains that persisted six weeks later and scaled with the designed engagement level, from 8 to 51 percentage points; (2) students in every condition self-reported sustained voluntary use, and confidence grew in step with skill; and (3) final examination performance did not differ between conditions, placing the possible boundary of the effects at the pathway from prompting skill to achievement. These findings provide instructors with an empirically calibrated set of options for translating GenAI-use policies into classroom practice.
item.dc:creator: Ruiwei Xiao, Runlong Ye, Xinying Hou, Jessica Wen, Harsh Kumar, Michael Liut, John Stamper

item.title: Knowing When to Move: Evidence Accumulation Models of Human Behavior in Traffic
item.description: arXiv:2606.00727v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Evidence accumulation models (EAMs) describe decisions as noisy evidence accumulating toward a decision boundary. Although widely studied in laboratory tasks, their application to dynamic, real-world behavior has received less attention. Traffic offers a setting where evidence changes as situations unfold, response timing matters, and decisions occur within ongoing control and interaction. This semi-systematic review synthesizes 28 publications (2014-2026) that model traffic decisions and control actions with EAMs. We organize the literature by modeling level (discrete decisions versus continuous action control) and implementation (stand-alone accumulators versus models embedded in broader perception-action or interaction frameworks). We examine how model components are implemented and evaluated across tasks. Overall, EAMs account for a range of dynamic road-user behaviors. Several comparisons suggest that response timing is better described by accumulating evidence as situations develop than by fixed delays or thresholds on momentary evidence, although accumulation models do not consistently outperform other kinds of models. Whether decreasing boundaries improve the fit differs between studies, and the models offer testable accounts of how decision-relevant information is processed. For cognitive scientists, traffic offers a testbed for studying how evidence from changing environments shapes decision-making. For applied modelers, the findings show how EAM components can be adapted to different traffic tasks, and why the choice of components needs to be evaluated for each task. However, most publications that estimated parameters pooled across participants, and most were not tested beyond the data they were fitted to, highlighting the value of participant-level or hierarchical estimation and of testing on new data.
